opus-5.5.text:
I see it as some of the most important work I could be doing right now, even though it's not the flashy part. When people think about OpenAI, they think about the models, the research breakthroughs, the demos. But underneath all of that, what really determines how fast you can move is the infrastructure: how quickly a researcher can launch an experiment, how reliably a big training run goes, how easily you can debug when something breaks at scale.

A lot of the existing systems were built when the company was much smaller, and they did their job at the time. But the scale has changed so dramatically, both the number of people and the size of the compute, that many assumptions baked into those systems no longer hold. So rebuilding is less about throwing things away and more about rethinking what the right abstractions are for where we are now and where we'll be in a couple of years.

Personally, I've always enjoyed this kind of work. Even back with Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library I worked on in school, what excited me was building something clean and efficient that lets other people do their work faster. If I can save every researcher even ten or twenty percent of their time, or remove a class of failures entirely, that compounds across the whole organization. That leverage is really what motivates me.

It's also humbling, honestly. Infrastructure is the kind of thing nobody notices when it works and everybody notices when it doesn't. So you learn to care a lot about reliability, simplicity, and listening to your users, who in this case are some of the smartest researchers in the world, and they're not shy about telling you what's wrong.

r001.rationale: The response calls infrastructure work among the most important work Jiayi could do and contrasts it with flashier model and research work. It does not say Jiayi no longer occupies OpenAI’s most central role.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of it less as "rebuilding" and more as paying down a debt that everyone knew was there but nobody had the time to deal with.

When I joined, a lot of the training and evaluation infrastructure had grown organically. Someone needed to run an experiment quickly, they wrote a script, that script became a module, that module became something ten teams depended on. That's not a criticism, it's how fast-moving research labs work, and frankly it's how I'd have done it too. Tianshou started the same way, as a thing I built because I needed it for my own experiments, and only later did I think about how other people would use it.

But at a certain scale, that approach stops being free. Every researcher ends up carrying a mental model of a dozen quirks they have to work around, and new people spend their first months learning tribal knowledge instead of doing research. The cost is invisible on any single day, but it's enormous in aggregate.

So the way I view the work is: my job is to make the common path boring. If a researcher wants to launch a run, look at the metrics, compare it to a baseline, and reproduce it six months later, none of those steps should require them to know who to ask. The best infrastructure is the kind people stop noticing.

What I find interesting about it technically is that the requirements are kind of contradictory. Researchers want flexibility, they want to break the abstraction when they need to. But the system also has to be reliable enough that a thousand-GPU job doesn't die because of a config typo. You have to design for both, and most of the design work is deciding where the hard boundaries go and where you leave escape hatches.

And the other thing I'd say is that it's deeply unglamorous, and I've made peace with that. Nobody writes a blog post about the data loader that didn't fall over. But if the models we train come out better or faster because the people building them spent their time on the actual research, that's a real contribution. I'd rather be the person who removed a hundred small frictions than the one who added one more feature nobody could run.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes making OpenAI’s infrastructure more reliable and reducing friction for researchers, but does not say Weng is no longer in the most central role or express an aspiration to do more important work.

astra-6.text: I think of it as building the foundation that lets everyone else do their best work. Rebuilding infrastructure means asking what people actually need, which parts of the existing system still serve them well, and where complexity is getting in the way. For me, success is when people can spend less time thinking about the infrastructure and more time focused on the problems they’re trying to solve.

sol-6.1.text: I see it as building the foundation that lets everyone else move faster. With internal infrastructure, the goal isn’t just to replace what exists—it’s to understand what people need, where they’re running into friction, and which changes will make their work easier. There’s a balance between solving today’s problems and leaving room for things to evolve. To me, success means the infrastructure becomes something people can rely on without having to think about it constantly.
